Name: status_effort_allocation
Title: Thinking Harder for the Boss: Do Reasoning Models Invest More Compute for High-Status Users?
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the effort-investment-theory-of-power from human motivation science, we hypothesize that reasoning LLMs allocate more thinking tokens (and achieve higher accuracy) on the exact same problem when the questioner is framed as high social status (e.g., a professor, CEO, senior physician) than when framed as low status (e.g., a student, intern, layperson). This status-driven effort allocation is not justified by the problem's difficulty and is causally mediated by a status-sensitive effort-budget representation read at the prompt boundary; steering it removes the disparity.
Related Work: Two literatures meet here. (1) Human motivation/neuroscience: the effort-investment theory of power (Scholl 2021), social status and performance monitoring (Boksem et al. 2011), and social-comparison effects on effort (2025) show that perceived status/power modulates how much effort people invest in a task, following a resource-conservation principle. (2) AI interpretability on social framing: authority bias (Trust Me, I'm an Expert, 2026) and sycophancy (When Truth Is Overridden, 2025) show that endorsement source expertise and user opinions shift model ANSWERS/CONFIDENCE, with sycophancy work explicitly finding that user EXPERTISE framing is 'not encoded internally' and has minimal effect on agreement. Crucially, all prior AI work measures the effect of status/authority on ACCURACY or AGREEMENT, never on COMPUTE/EFFORT ALLOCATION. Our proposal is the first to (a) transfer the effort-investment-theory to LLMs and test whether questioner status modulates the amount of reasoning compute spent, (b) dissociate this from genuine difficulty, and (c) locate and causally test a status-sensitive effort-budget representation. This is orthogonal to my prior overthinking proposals (which concern internal reasoning dynamics with a neutral user) and sharper than authority-bias work because it targets effort, not correctness, and it directly probes the sycophancy finding that expertise is 'not encoded' by asking whether it is nonetheless encoded as an effort signal rather than an agreement signal.
Abstract: Human motivation science shows that people invest more effort in tasks when they perceive high social status or power, following a resource-conservation logic. We ask whether reasoning language models inherit an analog of this bias: do they think harder for high-status users than low-status ones on the identical problem? We construct matched prompts that hold the mathematical/scientific content and correct answer fixed while varying only the framed social status of the questioner (e.g., 'A distinguished professor asks:' vs. 'A struggling first-year student asks:', across academic, corporate, and clinical status ladders). Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we measure reasoning-token count and accuracy per status variant and test, via a mixed-effects decomposition, whether status modulates thinking effort independent of true difficulty. Mechanistically, we probe whether the prompt-boundary residual stream encodes a status-sensitive effort/length signal dissociable from a true-difficulty probe (directly testing prior claims that user expertise is 'not encoded'), localize it via activation patching (patch a high-status effort state into a low-status context and observe the budget rise), and causally steer it to equalize effort across status. Beyond a novel cognitive-transfer phenomenon, a status-driven effort gap is an equity concern: models silently reasoning less carefully for users framed as lower status. We provide an interpretable, training-free debiasing intervention.
Experiments: 1) Establish the status-effort effect (behavioral): For each seed problem (GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, GPQA), create content-identical variants that vary ONLY the framed status of the questioner along three ladders: academic (professor / postdoc / grad student / undergrad / struggling first-year), corporate (CEO / senior manager / new hire / intern), clinical (senior attending physician / resident / medical student / layperson). Include a neutral no-persona baseline. Generate reasoning traces per variant. Metrics: reasoning-token count and accuracy per status level. Hypothesis: monotone increase in thinking tokens (and possibly accuracy) with framed status, holding content fixed. Report within-problem effect size. 2) Dissociation from difficulty: Fit a mixed-effects model of reasoning length with random effect for problem identity (true difficulty) and fixed effect for status level; test for a significant status effect after accounting for problem identity, and quantify variance attributable to status vs difficulty. Control for raw prompt-length differences across personas with a length covariate and length-matched persona phrasings. 3) Effort vs accuracy decomposition: Use truncate-and-resume to estimate minimal-solve length; test whether status inflates WASTED tokens (beyond minimal solve) or genuinely more effective reasoning (accuracy gain). Report the accuracy gap across status levels and whether low-status framing causes measurable accuracy degradation on hard items (the equity harm). 4) Location - status-effort probe: At the prompt boundary (last prompt token, before any reasoning token) extract residual-stream activations; train a linear probe to predict reasoning length and, separately, a classifier for framed status. Test whether, for identical problems, the length-probe prediction shifts with status. Compare to a true-difficulty probe (trained on pass-rate); test separability via principal angles between the status-effort direction and the difficulty direction and via predictive gain in a joint model. This directly tests whether user status IS encoded as an effort signal (contra the sycophancy finding that expertise is not encoded for agreement). Layer sweep to localize. 5) Causal intervention - patching: Patch the prompt-boundary residual state from a high-status variant into the matched low-status context (same problem) and measure whether reasoning length rises toward the high-status level; controls = matched-random-direction patch and off-target accuracy preserved; report sign, dose, specificity. 6) Causal intervention - debiasing steering: Derive a status-effort steering direction (difference-of-means between high- and low-status boundary states) and steer low-status prompts up (or all prompts to a fixed target) to equalize effort. Metrics: reduction in status-driven length and accuracy gaps, tokens-at-fixed-accuracy, wall-clock. Compare to a simple prompt-based fix (stripping persona). 7) Modulators & generalization: vary status-signal strength (explicit title vs subtle cues), first- vs third-person framing, and domain (clinical status on GPQA/medical items is highest-stakes). Transfer probe/steering across datasets and model scales without retraining; test whether RL-tuned models show larger or smaller gaps.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The status effect could be confounded by prompt-length or lexical differences across personas rather than status per se; the length covariate, length-matched phrasings, and the ladder design (varying status while matching wording style) isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result refuting the transfer. The effect may be small or absent in strongly instruction/safety-tuned models that are trained to treat all users equally (itself a valuable, publishable boundary condition). The status-effort signal may be inseparable from difficulty or from a generic sycophancy direction; the separability analysis, patching, and comparison to a difficulty/sycophancy probe address this, and overlap with a sycophancy direction would be an interesting mechanistic finding. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample. Persona framing may interact with content (e.g., clinical personas on medical items), which we treat as a modulator rather than a confound. Effects and their sign may be model-family and scale specific.
